projectile-motion.title: Projectile Motion Quiz
projectile-motion.description: Test your understanding of trajectories, range, and time of flight

questions.question: A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff with an initial velocity of 10 m/s. What is the horizontal acceleration of the ball during its flight? (Ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: In projectile motion with no air resistance, there is no horizontal acceleration. The only acceleration is gravity (9.8 m/s²) acting vertically downward. The horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

questions.question: At what launch angle will a projectile achieve maximum range on level ground?
questions.explanation: A projectile launched at 45° achieves maximum range on level ground. This is because sin(2θ) in the range equation R = (v₀²sin(2θ))/g reaches its maximum value of 1 when θ = 45°.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at an angle above the horizontal. At the highest point of its trajectory, which statement is true?
options: Both horizontal and vertical velocities are zero
The vertical velocity is zero, but horizontal velocity is not
The horizontal velocity is zero, but vertical velocity is not
Both velocities are at their maximum
questions.explanation: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, the vertical velocity becomes zero (the projectile momentarily stops rising before falling). However, the horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight, as there is no horizontal acceleration.

questions.question: Two projectiles are launched with the same initial speed. One is launched at 30° and the other at 60°. How do their ranges compare?
questions.explanation: Launch angles that are complementary (add up to 90°) produce the same range. Since 30° + 60° = 90°, both projectiles will have the same range. This is because sin(60°) = sin(120°) and sin(2×30°) = sin(60°) = sin(2×60°) = sin(120°).

questions.question: If you double the initial velocity of a projectile (keeping the angle constant), how does the maximum height change?
questions.explanation: Maximum height H = (v₀²sin²(θ))/(2g). Since H is proportional to v₀², doubling the initial velocity quadruples the maximum height.

questions.question: A soccer ball is kicked at ground level with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at 30° above horizontal. What is its vertical component of velocity? (sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: The vertical component of velocity is v₀sin(θ) = 20 × sin(30°) = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true about projectile motion (ignoring air resistance)?
questions.explanation: The total velocity does NOT remain constant in projectile motion. While horizontal velocity stays constant and vertical acceleration is constant, the vertical velocity changes continuously due to gravity, which changes the magnitude of total velocity.

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally from a 20m high cliff. If it takes 2 seconds to hit the ground, what was its initial horizontal velocity? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: We cannot determine the horizontal velocity from the given information. The time to fall depends only on the height and gravity (vertical motion), not on horizontal velocity. We would need to know the horizontal distance traveled to calculate the horizontal velocity.

questions.question: For a projectile launched at 45° with initial speed v₀, what fraction of the maximum height is reached at half the range?
questions.explanation: At 45° launch angle, the trajectory is symmetric. The maximum height occurs at exactly half the range, so at half the range, the projectile is at its maximum height. Therefore, the fraction is 1 (or 100%).

questions.question: Two projectiles are launched simultaneously from the same point. One is launched horizontally at 10 m/s, the other straight upward at 10 m/s. Which statement is true?
options: They hit the ground at the same time
They reach the same maximum height
questions.explanation: The horizontally launched projectile starts falling immediately, while the upward-launched one must first decelerate, stop, then fall. The horizontal projectile has less vertical distance to cover from its starting point and begins descending immediately, so it hits the ground first.

simple-pendulum.title: Simple Pendulum Quiz
simple-pendulum.description: Test your understanding of periodic motion and pendulum dynamics

questions.question: What is the period of a simple pendulum with length 1m on Earth? (g ≈ 10 m/s², π ≈ 3.14)
If you quadruple the length of a pendulum, how does the period change?
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), the period is proportional to √L. If L becomes 4L, then T becomes √4 × T = 2T. The period doubles.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect the period of a simple pendulum?
questions.explanation: From the formula T = 2π√(L/g) we see that the mass does not play a role in the period length so the answer is mass.

questions.question: What happens to the period of a pendulum if you take it to the Moon (where g is about 1/6 of Earth's gravity)?
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), if g becomes g/6, then T becomes √6 times larger. T_moon = 2π√(L/(g/6)) = √6 × 2π√(L/g) ≈ 2.45 × T_earth.

questions.question: For a simple pendulum, the small angle approximation assumes that sin(θ) ≈ θ. This approximation works well til approximately:
questions.explanation: The small angle approximation works well till about 15 degrees then the margin of error becomes too big and the formula doesn't work anymore.

questions.question: A pendulum swings back and forth, completing 20 oscillations in 40 seconds. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency f = number of oscillations / time = 20 / 40s. So the answer is 0.5Hz.

questions.question: At the maximum displacement (amplitude) of a pendulum's swing, which of these is correct?
options: Velocity is maximum, acceleration is zero
Velocity is zero, acceleration is maximum
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Both velocity and acceleration are maximum
questions.explanation: At maximum displacement, the pendulum momentarily stops (velocity = 0) before changing direction. At this point, the restoring force and therefore acceleration are at their maximum values, pulling the bob back toward equilibrium.

questions.question: If you double the mass of a pendulum bob while keeping length constant, what happens to the maximum speed of the bob during its swing?
questions.explanation: For the same amplitude, the maximum speed remains the same. From energy conservation: v_max = √(2gh), which depends only on the height difference (amplitude), not on mass. The period also doesn't change with mass.

questions.question: A grandfather clock uses a pendulum to keep time. If the clock runs slow, what adjustment should be made?
options: Increase the mass of the bob
Decrease the mass of the bob
questions.explanation: If the clock runs slow, the period is too long (T = 2π√(L/g)). To decrease the period, you must decrease the length L. Making the pendulum shorter will increase its frequency and make the clock run faster.

inclined-plane.title: Inclined Plane Quiz
inclined-plane.description: Test your understanding of forces, friction, and motion on slopes

questions.question: A block rests on a frictionless inclined plane at 30°. What is the acceleration of the block down the plane? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: On a frictionless incline, a = g sin(θ) = 10 × sin(30°) = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s². The acceleration depends only on the angle and gravity when there's no friction.

questions.question: A 10 kg block sits on an incline at 30°. What is the component of the weight parallel to the incline? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: The parallel component is F∥ = mg sin(θ) = 10 kg × 10 m/s² × sin(30°) = 100 × 0.5 = 50 N. This is the component that pulls the block down the slope.

questions.question: Which statement is true about the normal force on an inclined plane?
options: It equals the weight of the object
It is always less than the weight
It is perpendicular to the incline surface
It increases as the angle decreases
questions.explanation: The normal force is always perpendicular to the surface of contact. On an incline, N = mg cos(θ), which is less than the full weight mg. As angle increases, normal force decreases.

questions.question: A block is on a 45° incline and has a coefficient of static friction μ = 0.5. Will the block slide?
options: Cannot determine without knowing the normal force
questions.explanation: The block slides if tan(θ) > μ. Since tan(45°) = 1 and μ = 0.5. The block will slide.

questions.question: What happens to normal force as the angle of an inclined plane increases from 0° to 90°
questions.explanation: Normal force N = mg cos(θ). At θ = 0° (horizontal), cos(0°) = 1, so N = mg. At θ = 90° (vertical), cos(90°) = 0, so N = 0. The normal force decreases from mg to 0.

questions.question: A box slides down a 30° incline with kinetic friction coefficient μ = 0.2. What is its acceleration? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866)
questions.explanation: With friction: a = g(sin(θ) - μ cos(θ)) = 10(0.5 - 0.2 × 0.866) = 10(0.5 - 0.173) = 10(0.327) = 3.27 m/s². Friction opposes motion, reducing acceleration.

questions.question: Two identical blocks are placed on inclines of diffrerent angles. Which experiences a greater normal force?
options: The block with a steeper incline
The block on the less steep incline
Both experience the same normal force
Depends on the material of the block
questions.explanation: Since N = mg cos(θ), and cosine decreases as angle increases, the block on the less steep incline will a greater normal force. Material doesn't effect this relationship.

questions.question: At what angle will a block just begin to slide if the coefficient of static friction is 0.577? (tan⁻¹(0.577) ≈ 30°)
questions.explanation: A block just begins to slide when tan(θ) = μ. If μ = 0.577, then θ = tan⁻¹(0.577) = 30°. At angles greater than 30°, the block will slide; at smaller angles, it remains stationary.

questions.question: A block slides from rest down a frictionless 4-meter long incline at 30°. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: Using energy: mgh = ½mv², where h = L sin(θ) = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m. So v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 2) = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s. Alternatively, use kinematics with a = 5 m/s².

questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect the acceleration of a block sliding down a frictionless incline?
questions.explanation: Since a = g sin(θ), acceleration depends only on g and θ. Mass cancels out in the equation (F = ma becomes mg sin(θ) = ma, so a = g sin(θ)). Length affects time but not acceleration.

spring-mass-system.title: Spring-Mass System Quiz
spring-mass-system.description: Test your understanding of harmonic motion, Hooke's law, and oscillations

questions.question: A spring with spring constant k = 100 N/m is compressed by 0.2m. What is the restoring force?
questions.explanation: Using Hooke's law F = kx = 100 N/m × 0.2 m = 20 N. The negative sign in F = -kx indicates the force opposes the displacement, but the magnitude is 20 N.

questions.question: If you quadruple the mass attached to a spring while keeping the spring constant the same, how does the period change?
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(m/k), the period is proportional to √m. If m becomes 4m, then the period doubles

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT effect the period of a spring-mass system?
questions.explanation: From T = 2π√(m/k), we see that period depends only on mass and spring constant. The amplitude does not affect the period in simple harmonic motion.

questions.question: At what point in its oscillations does a spring-mass system have maximum kinetic energy?
options: At any point, kinetic energy is constant
questions.explanation: At the equilibrium position (x = 0), all energy is kinetic since potential energy is zero. The mass moves fastest through equilibrium, so kinetic energy is maximum. At maximum displacement, the mass momentarily stops (KE = 0).

questions.question: If you double both mass and the spring constant, what happens to the period?
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(m/k). If both m and k are doubled: T_new = 2π√(2m/2k) = 2π√(m/k) = T. The period stays the same because the ratio m/k remains unchanged.

questions.question: A spring-mass system oscillates with amplitude A. At what displacement from equilibrium is the speed equal to half the maximum speed?
questions.explanation: Using energy conservation: ½kA² = ½kx² + ½mv². When v = v_max/2, solving gives x = A√3/2 ≈ 0.866A. At this position, the kinetic energy is 1/4 of maximum kinetic energy.

questions.question: What is the total mechanical energy of a spring-mass system with spring constant 200 N/m oscillating with amplitude 0.1 m?
questions.explanation: Total energy E = ½kA² = ½(200)(0.1)² = ½(200)(0.01) = 1 J. In the absence of friction, this energy remains constant throughout the oscillation, converting between kinetic and potential energy.

questions.question: Two identical springs (k₁ = k₂ = k) are connected in series and support a mass m. What is the effective spring constant?
questions.explanation: For springs in series, 1/k_eff = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ = 1/k + 1/k = 2/k, so k_eff = k/2. Springs in series are easier to stretch (lower effective spring constant) than a single spring.

questions.question: A horizontal spring-mass system oscillates on a frictionless surface. If the same system were oriented vertically, how would the period compare?
questions.explanation: The period T = 2π√(m/k) is independent of gravity and orientation. In the vertical case, gravity only shifts the equilibrium position but doesn't change the period. The restoring force still follows Hooke's law around the new equilibrium.

elastic-collisions.title: Elastic Collisions Quiz
elastic-collisions.description: Test your understanding of momentum conservation, kinetic energy, and collision dynamics

questions.question: Which quantities are conserved in an elastic collision?
questions.explanation: In an elastic collision both are conserved, those are the most important rules to remember in elastic collisions.

questions.question: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides elastically with a stationary 2 kg ball. What are the final velocities?
options: First stops, second moves at 6 m/s
First moves at 2 m/s, second at 4 m/s
First moves at -6 m/s, second at 0 m/s
questions.explanation: For equal masses in 1D elastic collision where one has a speed, and the other is stationary, the moving one will transfer all the velocity to the stationary one.

questions.question: WHat is the coefficient of restitution for a perfectly elastic collision?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of restitution is e = 1 for a perfectly elastic collision.

questions.question: A 4 kg object moving at 8 m/s collides elastically with a stationary 2 kg object. What is the velocity of the 4 kg object after collision?
questions.explanation: Using v₁f = ((m₁-m₂)v₁ᵢ)/(m₁+m₂) = ((4-2)×8)/(4+2) = 16/6 = 2.67 m/s. The heavier object continues in the same direction but at reduced speed after transferring momentum to the lighter object.

questions.question: In a head-on elastic collision between two object of equal mass, where both are initially moving toward each other with equal speeds, what happens?
options: They bounce back with their initial speeds reversed
They both continue moving forward at reduced speeds
One stops and one moves forward
questions.explanation: With equal masses and equal but opposite velocities, after an elastic collision each object reverses direction and maintains its original speed. This is due to symmetry of the collision and conservation laws.

questions.question: A ball of mass m moving at velocity v collides elastically with an identical stationary ball. How much kinetic energy does the moving ball transfer?
questions.explanation: For equal masses with one initially at rest, the moving ball transfers 100% of its kinetic energy to the stationary ball. The first ball stops completely (KE = 0) and the second ball moves with the original velocity.

questions.question: What happens when a very light object collides elastically with a very heavy stationary object?
options: The light object bounces back with nearly the same speed
questions.explanation: When m₁ << m₂ and m₂ is at rest, the light object bounces back with approximately v₁f ≈ -v₁ᵢ (reversed direction, same speed), while the heavy object barely moves. Think of a ball bouncing off a wall.

questions.question: Two objects undergo an elastic collision. If the total momentum before collision is 20 kg·m/s, what is the total momentum after collision?
questions.explanation: Momentum is always conserved in collisions (both elastic and inelastic). If the initial total momentum is 20 kg·m/s, the final total momentum must also be 20 kg·m/s.

questions.question: A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides elastically with a 1 kg ball moving in the opposite direction at 2 m/s. What is the total momentum of the system?
questions.explanation: Taking the 3 kg ball's direction as positive: p_total = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = 3(4) + 1(-2) = 12 - 2 = 10 kg·m/s. This momentum is conserved throughout the collision.

questions.question: In a 1D elastic collision, the relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation. If two balls approach each other at a relative velocity of 10 m/s, at what relative velocity do they separate?
questions.explanation: For elastic collisions, |v₁ᵢ - v₂ᵢ| = |v₂f - v₁f|. The magnitude of relative velocity is preserved, so they separate at 10 m/s. This is a fundamental property of elastic collisions and relates to e = 1.

circular-motion.title: Circula Motion Quiz
circular-motion.description: Test your understanding of centripical force, angular velocity, and rotational dynamics

questions.question: A car travels around a circular track of raduis 50 m at a constant speed of 20m/s. What is its centripental acceleration?
questions.explanation: Using a_c = v²/r = (20)²/50 = 400/50 = 8 m/s². This acceleration is directed toward the center of the circular path and is constant in magnitude but continuously changing in direction.

questions.question: What provides the centripental force for a car makeing a turn on the road?
questions.explanation: Friction between the tires and road provides the centripental force needed for turning. Without sufficient friction (like on ice), the car cannot turn effectively and will sile outward.

questions.question: If you double the speed of an object in circular motion while keeping the radius constant, how does that affect the centripental force?
questions.explanation: Since F_c = mv²/r, the centripental force is proportional to v². So if the speed doubles, 2² = 4, F_c quadruples.

questions.question: An object completes 10 revolutions in 5 seconds. What is it's frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency f = number of oscillations / time = 10 / 5s. So the answer is 2Hz.

questions.question: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string is swung in a horizontal circle at 4 m/s. What is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation: The tension provides the centripental force F_c = mv²/r = 0.5 × (4)² / 1 = 0.5 × 16 / 1 = 8 N. The tension must equal the required centripetal force to maintain circular motion.

questions.question: What is the direction of the centripental acceleration in uniform circular motion?
options: Towaard the center of the circle
Away from the center of the circle
questions.explanation: Centripental acceleration always points toward the center of the circular path. This is what causes the object to continuously change direction and move in a circle rather then a straight line

questions.question: A sitelite orbits the Earth at a constant speed. Which statement is true?
options: Its speed is constant but velocity is changing
Both spee dand velocity are changing
questions.explanation: Speed(magnitude) is constant, but velocity (which includesa direction) is continuously changing because the satelite is always changing direction.

questions.question: A wheel of radius 0.5 m rotates with angular velocity 4 rad/s. What is the tangential speed of a point on its rim?
questions.explanation: Using v = rω = 0.5 m × 4 rad/s = 2 m/s. The tangential speed is the linear speed of a point on the rim, perpendicular to the radius.

questions.question: At the top of a vertical circular loop, a roller coaster car experiences a normal force of zero. What is the car's speed? (r = 10 m, g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: At the top with N = 0, gravity alone provides centripetal force: mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √(10 × 10) = √100 = 10 m/s. This is the minimum speed to maintain contact with the track at the top.

questions.question: Two points on a rotating disk are located at distances r and 2r from the center. How do their angular velocities compare?
options: The outer point has twice the angular velocity
The inner point has twice the angular velocity
Both have the same angular velocity
The outer point has four times the angular velocity
questions.explanation: All points on a rigid rotating object have the same angular velocity ω. However, their tangential speeds differ: v = rω, so the outer point moves twice as fast linearly but rotates at the same angular rate.

orbital-mechanics.title: Obrital Mechanics Quiz
orbital-mechanics.description: Test your understanding of satalites, gravitatonal orbits, and Kepler's laws
keyConcepts: Kepler's trhee laws of planatery momentum

questions.question: Which of Kepler's laws states that planets sweep out equal areas in equal times?
questions.explanation: Kepler's second law (Law of Equal Areas) states that a line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. This means planets move faster when closer to the Sun and slower when farther away.

questions.question: If a satelite's orbital radius is increased by a factor of 4, how does its orbital period change?
questions.explanation: Kepler's third law stats, line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. This means planets move faster when closer to the Sun and slower when farther away.

questions.question: What is the relationship between orbital velocity and escape velocity from the same point
questions.explanation: Since v_orbital = √(GM/r) and v_escape = √(2GM/r), we have v_escape = √2 × v_orbital ≈ 1.414 × v_orbital. Escape velocity is always √2 times the orbital velocity at the same radius.

questions.question: A geostationary satallite orbits Earth with a period of 24 hours. What is special about its orbit?
options: It appears stationary relative to Earth's surface
It has the lowest possible orbital altitude
It moves faster then Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: A geostationary satallite orbits above the equator with a 24-hour period, mathing Earth's rotation. This makes it appear stationary relative to a point on Earth.

questions.question: If a satellite's orbital radius doubles, how does its orbital velocity change?
questions.explanation: From v = √(GM/r), velocity is proportional to 1/√r. If r doubles, v becomes v/√2 ≈ 0.707v. The satellite moves slower at higher orbits because gravitational force is weaker.

questions.question: What provides the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in orbit around Earth?
questions.explanation: The gravitational force from Earth provides the centripetal force needed for orbital motion. In a stable orbit, F_gravity = F_centripetal, which gives us mv²/r = GMm/r², leading to the orbital velocity formula.

questions.question: According to Kepler's first law, the orbit of a planet is:
options: A perfect circle with the Sun at the center
An ellipse with the Sun at one focus
A parabola with the Sun at the vertex
A hyperbola with the Sun at one focus
questions.explanation: Kepler's first law states that planets orbit in ellipses with the Sun at one of the two foci (not at the center). While some orbits are nearly circular, they are technically elliptical.

questions.question: Two satellites orbit Earth at different altitudes. The satellite at lower altitude has:
questions.explanation: Lower orbits require higher speeds (v = √(GM/r) increases as r decreases) and have shorter periods (T ∝ r^(3/2)). The satellite closer to Earth must move faster to maintain its orbit and completes orbits more quickly.

questions.question: The total mechanical energy of a satellite in a circular orbit is:
questions.explanation: Total energy E = KE + PE = ½mv² - GMm/r. For a circular orbit, this simplifies to E = -GMm/(2r), which is negative. Negative total energy indicates the satellite is gravitationally bound to Earth.

questions.question: If Earth's mass were doubled while its radius remained the same, how would the escape velocity change?
questions.explanation: Since v_escape = √(2GM/r), escape velocity is proportional to √M. If M doubles, v_escape becomes √2 × v_escape ≈ 1.414 times the original value.

rotational-dynamics.title: Rotational Dynamics Quiz
rotational-dynamics.description: Test your understanding of torque, moment of inertia, and angular momentum
keyConcepts: Moment of inertia for different shapes

questions.question: A force of 10 N is applied perpendicular to a wrench 0.3m from the pivot point. What is the torque produced?
questions.explanation: Using τ = rF sin(θ), where θ = 90° (perpendicular): τ = 0.3 m × 10 N × sin(90°) = 0.3 × 10 × 1 = 3 N·m. The torque represents the rotational effect of the force.

questions.question: Which object has the largest moment of inertia about its center? (If all have the same M and R)
questions.explanation: The thin ring has I = MR², which is the largest. Moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed from the rotation axis. The ring has all its mass at maximum distance R, giving it the highest moment of inertia.

questions.question: If a figure skater pulls her arm inward during a spin, what happens to her angular velocity?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved. When she pulls her arms in, her moment of inertia I decreases. To keep L constant, her angular velocity ω must increase, making her spin faster.

questions.question: A disk and a hoop of equal mass and radius roll down an incline without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
options: They reach at the same time
Depends on the angle of incline
questions.explanation: The disk reaches first because it has a smaller moment of inertia (I_disk = ½MR² vs I_hoop = MR²). Less rotational inertia means more energy goes into translational motion, resulting in higher acceleration down the incline.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of torque?
questions.explanation: Torque has units of N·m (newton-meters). Although this has the same dimensions as joules (energy), torque and energy are different physical quantities, so N·m is preferred over J for torque.

questions.question: A wheel with moment of inertia 2 kg·m² rotates at 5 rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Using KE_rot = ½Iω² = ½(2 kg·m²)(5 rad/s)² = ½(2)(25) = 25 J. This represents the energy due to the rotational motion of the wheel.

questions.question: Two forces of equal magnitude are applied to a door. One is applied perpendicular to the door at the edge, the other at 45° to the door at the edge. Which produces greater torque?
options: Cannot determine without knowing the force magnitude
questions.explanation: Since τ = rF sin(θ), and sin(90°) = 1 > sin(45°) = 0.707, the perpendicular force produces greater torque. Maximum torque occurs when force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm.

questions.question: A solid cylinder and a hollow cylinder of the same mass and radius are released from rest at the top of an incline. Assuming they roll without slipping, which statement is true?
options: The solid cylinder reaches the bottom with greater velocity
The hollow cylinder reaches the bottom with greater velocity
Both reach the bottom with the same velocity
Both reach the bottom with the same kinetic energy
questions.explanation: The solid cylinder has smaller moment of inertia (½MR² vs MR² for hollow), so more of its potential energy converts to translational kinetic energy rather than rotational. It reaches the bottom with greater velocity, though both have the same total energy.

questions.question: If you double the angular velocity of a rotating object while keeping its moment of inertia constant, how does the angular momentum change?
questions.explanation: Since L = Iω, angular momentum is directly proportional to angular velocity when I is constant. Doubling ω doubles L. Angular momentum is a linear function of angular velocity.

questions.question: A rod of length L and mass M rotates about one end. What is its moment of inertia about this axis?
questions.explanation: For a rod rotating about one end, I = (1/3)ML². This is larger than rotating about the center (I = (1/12)ML²) because the average distance of mass from the axis is greater when rotating about an end.

questions.question: What causes white light to split int odifferent colors when passing through a prism?
questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because the refractive index of the prism material varies with wavelength. Different colors (wavelengths) refract by different amoutns, causing white light to separate into component colors.

questions.question: Which color of visable light has the highest refractive index in glass?
questions.explanation: Violet light has the heighest refractive index in glass because it has the shortest waelength. The refractive index generally increases as wavelength decreases, so violet bends the most and red bends the least.

questions.question: A ray of light enters a glass prism with an angle of incidence of 30°. If the refractive index of glass is 1.5, what is the angle of refraction? (sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: Using Snell's law: 1.0 × sin(30°) = 1.5 × sin(θ₂), so 0.5 = 1.5 × sin(θ₂), giving sin(θ₂) = 0.333, thus θ₂ ≈ 19.5°. Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium.

questions.question: In a rainbow, which color appears on the outer edge?
questions.explanation: Red appears on the outer edge of a rainbow because it refracts the least in water droplets. The order from outer to inner is: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV).

questions.question: What is the angle of minimum deviation for a prism?
options: The smallest angle between incident and emergent rays
The largest angle between incident and emergent rays
When the angle of incidence is 90°
When the light does not refract
questions.explanation: Minimum deviation occurs when the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base, making the angle of incidence equal to the angle of emergence. This produces the smallest deviation angle between incident and emergent rays.

questions.question: A prism has a refracting angle of 60°. If the refractive index is 1.5, what is the approximate angle of minimum deviation?
questions.explanation: Using δ_min ≈ (n - 1)A for small angles: δ_min = (1.5 - 1) × 60° = 0.5 × 60° = 30°. The minimum deviation depends on both the prism angle and the refractive index.

questions.question: Why doesn't a rectangular glass slab produce dispersion like a prism does?
options: The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, canceling dispersion
Rectangular slabs have no refractive index variation
Glass slabs only work with monochromatic light
questions.explanation: Although dispersion occurs at the first surface of a glass slab, the second refraction cancels this effect. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray with only lateral displacement, so the colors recombine.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for observing a rainbow?
options: Sun in front of the observer
Refraction and internal reflection in droplets
questions.explanation: For a rainbow to be visible, the Sun must be behind the observer. Sunlight refracts entering the water droplet, reflects internally, and refracts again upon exiting, with the observer seeing the dispersed light.

questions.question: If a prism is immersed in water (n = 1.33) instead of air, what happens to the dispersion?
questions.explanation: Dispersion decreases because the relative refractive index (n_glass/n_water) is smaller than (n_glass/n_air). The difference in refraction between colors is reduced, resulting in less separation of the spectrum.

questions.question: What is the sequence of colors in the visible spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength?
options: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red
Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet
questions.explanation: The visible spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength is: Red (≈700 nm), Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (≈400 nm). This is remembered by the acronym ROYGBIV.

standing-waves.title: Standing Waves Quiz
keyConcepts: Standing waves in strings and pipes

formulas.description: Wavelength for string fixed at both ends
Wavelength for pipe open at one end (n odd)

questions.question: Standing waves are formed by the interference of:
options: Two waves travelling in the same direction
Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
A single wave reflecting off a barrier
questions.explanation: Standing waves form when two identical waves (same frequency and amplitude) traveling in opposite directions interfere. This typically occurs when a wave reflects back on itself, creating a pattern of nodes and antinodes.

questions.question: What is a node in a standing waves
options: A point where the wave speed is maximum
questions.explanation: A node is a point of zero displacement that remains stationary in a standing wave. Nodes occur where destructive interference is complete. They are separated by half a wavelength.

questions.question: A string fixed at both ends is 2 m long and vibrates in its fundamental mode. What is the wavelength of the standing wave?
questions.explanation: For the fundamental mode (n = 1) of a string fixed at both ends, λ = 2L = 2 × 2 m = 4 m. The fundamental mode has one antinode in the middle with nodes at both ends, fitting half a wavelength in the length.

questions.question: How many antinodes are present in the thrid harmonic of a string fixed at both ends?
questions.explanation: The third harmonic (n = 3) has 3 antinodes. The number of antinodes equals the harmonic number for a string fixed at both ends. It contains 1.5 complete wavelengths within the string length.

questions.question: If the fundamental frequency of a vibrating string is 100 Hz, what is the frequency of the second harmonic?
questions.explanation: For a string fixed at both ends, f_n = n × f_1. The second harmonic (n = 2) has frequency f_2 = 2 × 100 Hz = 200 Hz. Each harmonic is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.

questions.question: A pipe is open at one end and closed at the other. Which harmonics can it support?
questions.explanation: A pipe open at one end and closed at the other can only support odd harmonics (n = 1, 3, 5, ...). This is because it must have an antinode at the open end and a node at the closed end, which only allows odd multiples of λ/4.

questions.question: The distance between two consecutive nodes in a standing wave is:
questions.explanation: Consecutive nodes are separated by λ/2 (half a wavelength). Similarly, consecutive antinodes are also separated by λ/2, and the distance from a node to the nearest antinode is λ/4.

questions.question: A string of length 1.2 m vibrates at 300 Hz in its third harmonic. What is the wave speed on the string?
questions.explanation: For the third harmonic, λ = 2L/n = 2(1.2)/3 = 0.8 m. Using v = fλ = 300 Hz × 0.8 m = 240 m/s. The wave speed depends on the string's tension and mass per unit length.

questions.question: What happens to the fundamental frequency of a string if you double its tension while keeping length and mass constant?
questions.explanation: Wave speed v = √(T/μ), where T is tension. If tension doubles, v increases by √2. Since f = v/(2L), frequency also increases by √2. Doubling tension increases the fundamental frequency by approximately 1.414 times.

questions.question: A pipe open at both ends has a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz. What is the fundamental frequency of a pipe of the same length but closed at one end? (Same wave speed)
questions.explanation: For a pipe open at both ends, f = v/(2L). For a pipe closed at one end, f = v/(4L). Since v and L are the same, the closed pipe has half the frequency: 200 Hz / 2 = 100 Hz. The closed pipe fits only λ/4 instead of λ/2.

wave-interference.title: Wave Interference Quiz
wave-interference.discription: Test your understanding superposition, constructive and destructive interference

questions.question: What is the principle of superposition?
options: Waves cannot pass through each other
The resultant displacement is the sum of individual displacement
Waves always cancel each other out
Only waves of the same frequency can interfere
questions.explanation: The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. This principle allows both for constructive and destructive interference

questions.question: Constructive interference occurs when the path difference between two waves is:
questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when the path difference Δx = nλ, where n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ... This means the waves arrive in phase, and their amplitudes add together to produce maximum amplitude.

questions.question: What phase difference corresponds to destructive interference?
questions.explanation: Destructive interference occurs when the phase difference is an odd multiple of 180° (π radians): 180°, 540°, 900°, etc. This corresponds to waves being exactly out of phase, causing them to cancel each other.

questions.question: Two coherent sources produce waves with wavelength 2 m. What path difference produces the first destructive interference?
questions.explanation: The first destructive interference (n = 0) occurs at path difference Δx = (n + ½)λ = (0 + ½) × 2 m = 1 m. This is half a wavelength, which puts the waves exactly out of phase.

questions.question: In Young's double slit experiment, what happens to the fringe spacing if the wavelength of light is increased?
questions.explanation: Fringe spacing is given by Δy = λL/d, which is directly proportional to wavelength λ. If wavelength increases, the spacing between bright (or dark) fringes increases proportionally.

questions.question: What is required for two wave sources to be coherent?
options: Same frequency and constant phase relationship
questions.explanation: Coherent sources must have the same frequency and maintain a constant phase relationship. This ensures a stable interference pattern. Without coherence, the interference pattern would constantly shift and blur.

questions.question: In a double slit experiment, the distance between slits is 0.5 mm, screen distance is 2 m, and wavelength is 500 nm. What is the spacing between bright fringes?
questions.explanation: Using Δy = λL/d = (500 × 10⁻⁹ m × 2 m) / (0.5 × 10⁻³ m) = (1000 × 10⁻⁹) / (0.5 × 10⁻³) = 2 × 10⁻³ m = 2 mm. The fringe spacing is uniform across the pattern.

questions.question: Two waves with equal amplitudes A interfere constructively. What is the amplitude of the resultant wave?
questions.explanation: In constructive interference, the amplitudes add directly. Two waves of amplitude A produce a resultant amplitude of 2A. The intensity, which is proportional to amplitude squared, becomes 4 times larger.

questions.question: What type of interference occurs when the path difference is 2.5λ?
questions.explanation: A path difference of 2.5λ = (2 + 0.5)λ = (n + ½)λ where n = 2, which is the condition for destructive interference. The waves are out of phase by an odd multiple of π radians.

questions.question: In Young's double slit experiment, if the slit separation is doubled while keeping other factors constant, what happens to the fringe width?
questions.explanation: Fringe width Δy = λL/d is inversely proportional to slit separation d. If d is doubled, the fringe width is halved. The fringes become closer together, making the pattern more compressed.
